Thought: Controlled benchmark for writing OMIM-style entries from exactly the cited papers; only the generation strategy varies, with a single model (Claude Opus 5.5) doing generation, fact-list splitting, auditing and judging. The design is careful: fixed fact lists split once, completion treated as an outcome, replicate-noise floor, sensitivity analysis counting missing drafts as zero, a matched ablation separating intermediate representation from extraction effort, and an unusually candid limitations section. But the headline findings are (a) reading strategies are within ~1-2 points of each other and (b) full text beats abstracts by 44 points on facts derived from curator text written from full text. (b) is close to tautological given how the reference is built and echoes Cohen et al. 2010; (a) is a null at n=93 with a single model, and its generality is limited because 81% of papers are abstract/title only, which compresses differences (the paper itself shows gaps grow with full text). The whole measurement chain rests on an unvalidated same-family judge (fact splitting, present/absent judgements, audit, missed-fact attribution), with no human agreement study even on a small sample; this is the main soundness gap. Strategies were developed on the evaluation entries. The hidden-full-text experiment compares a repaired draft against unrepaired drafts. Planted-error test has no negative controls. ML novelty for ICLR is modest (no new method; implementations of existing paradigms); value is as a dataset/benchmark contribution, which depends on release, and curator text cannot be redistributed. Writing is precise but extremely dense with numbers. Table 1 'Supp.' column says after repair, yet memory-only is never repaired. Header still reads ICLR 2025. Leaning reject, persuadable with human validation and a second model.
Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded knowledge-base writing in clinical genetics: 100 OMIM phenotype entries (stratified by creation era, 2-12 references each) are each rewritten from their header and exactly the papers the curators cited, with the causal gene withheld, and only the generation strategy varies. One model (Claude Opus 5.5) performs every step under the same guards (ontology-search-constrained HPO IDs, HGNC normalisation, mandatory citations), claim-level audit with one repair round, and scoring. Strategies span three paradigms (direct long-context reading and an agentic curator; extract-then-write via an evidence graph or a per-patient case table; recall-then-verify), a memory-only control, and three add-ons (second-hand evidence from citing papers, a learned curation guide, and case reconciliation). The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', is coverage of fixed fact lists split once from OMIM allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar. Main findings: on 93 entries all strategies completed, reading strategies score 47.2-49.1% (replicate noise +/-1.0 point), memory-based ones ~15%; hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 77.4% to 31.2% (46 entries); differences between strategies grow with the share of full text; a matched ablation attributes much of the extract-then-write deficit to extraction effort; the audit catches 60/60 planted single-fact substitutions but checks fidelity to the cited source rather than correctness; second-hand evidence adds +1.8 points at a cost in unsupported claims; the learned guide and reconciliation are nulls.
Strengths: Clean experimental control: same papers, same model, same guards, audit and scoring, so the generation strategy is the only manipulated variable; this addresses a real comparability gap in the literature on document-to-structured-text systems.

Methodologically careful evaluation choices: fact lists are split once without sight of any draft and reused for all strategies (avoiding draft-adaptive denominators); completion, including safety-filter stops, is treated as an outcome and comparisons are restricted to jointly completed entries, with a missing-as-zero sensitivity analysis; paired bootstrap intervals, sign counts and Holm correction are reported.
A measured replicate-noise floor (three repeated runs on 30 entries) is used to calibrate small differences, which is rare and valuable in LLM-pipeline comparisons.

The within-paper full-text-hiding experiment and the missed-fact attribution (Figure 3) give a direct, paired answer to whether the bottleneck is the strategy or the input, rather than relying on cross-entry correlations.

The matched ablation (Table 2) honestly shows that the apparent deficit of extract-then-write partly reflects implementation choices (extraction effort), which tempers what would otherwise be an over-reaching negative claim about intermediate representations.

Unusually candid scoping and limitations: the paper repeatedly distinguishes 'judged supported' from correct, reports that the audit checks fidelity not truth (with the second-hand evidence case as a concrete demonstration), and states that no human validated any judgement.
Contamination check via creation-era bands plus a set of entries created after June 2026, showing memory contributes little for new entries while acknowledging this does not rule out memorisation.
Built entirely from public resources with per-entry release of drafts, verdicts and scores; costs and token counts are reported.
Weaknesses: No human validation anywhere in the measurement chain. The same model family writes the drafts, splits the curator paragraphs into facts, judges each fact present/partly/absent/contradicted, audits claims, attributes missed facts to available text, and adjudicates contradictions. Self-preference bias (which the paper cites) and systematic judge errors could shift all strategies in correlated ways or interact with strategy style (e.g. paraphrase-heavy vs. extraction-heavy outputs). Even a modest curator or expert agreement study (e.g. 200-500 fact judgements, a sample of audit verdicts) is needed before the primary endpoint can be trusted at the 1-2 point resolution the paper's conclusions rely on.

Single model, single family. The central claim that 'the reading strategies are close' is a statement about one frontier model with a very long context window; it is plausible that strategy matters much more for weaker or shorter-context models, so the generality and therefore significance of the main finding is limited. No second model (open-weight or another provider) was tested even on a subset.

The headline access result is close to expected by construction. The reference facts come from curator text written from full papers (often including supplementary data), so drafts from abstracts necessarily cannot convey most of them; that coverage falls from 77% to 31% largely restates that abstracts contain less than full text (cf. Cohen et al., 2010). The experiment is well executed, but its novelty as a finding is limited, and the comparison is further confounded because only the full-text draft went through the repair round.

The 'strategies are close' conclusion is drawn in a regime where 81% of papers are abstract- or title-only and entries have 2-12 references, which compresses differences; the paper itself shows differences of 2-6 points where more full text exists and does not test inputs too large for one prompt, which is precisely where intermediate representations and agentic reading are motivated. The main comparison therefore does not address the setting in which the compared designs are expected to differ.

The primary endpoint is narrow and indirect: variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs, not the narrative entry text, and drafts make about twice as many statements per paper as the reference has facts. Coverage thus rewards one kind of content and is silent on whether extra content is correct, relevant or redundant; precision against the reference is not reported for paragraph text.
No separate development set: strategies were designed and tuned on the evaluation entries, which may favour whichever strategies received more iteration (likely direct reading as the baseline).

The audit's planted-error test has no unaltered controls, so specificity / false-flag rate is unknown; only blunt single-fact substitutions were tested, and omissions and misattributions were not. The 60/60 sensitivity result is therefore weak evidence about audit quality.

Limited methodological novelty for ICLR: the strategies are re-implementations of existing paradigms, and the learned-guide and recall-then-verify implementations are deliberately minimal (two reflection rounds on 27 entries; recall-then-verify forbidden from adding content), so their nulls are largely uninformative. The contribution is primarily a domain benchmark and empirical study, whose value depends on adoption and on a reference that cannot itself be redistributed.

Presentation is very dense: almost every sentence carries several numbers and intervals, many important definitions and results are deferred to the appendix, and the reader must track several different entry subsets (100, 97, 96, 93, 49/46, 40/38, 30, 20). A short table of subsets and their purposes, and fewer numbers in the running text, would help.

Minor issues: Table 1's 'Supp.' column is described as 'after repair' but the memory-only control is never repaired; the running header reads 'ICLR 2025'; the agentic curator's interval (-1.3, +0.0) touches zero yet it is described as within noise while its sign counts (31/42/20) lean negative; the sensitivity analysis gives wide intervals (e.g. -3.0 to +3.1) that do not by themselves support 'the same picture'.
Questions: Can you provide any human (ideally curator or trained geneticist) agreement data for the fact-list splitting and the present/partly/absent judgements, even on a small random sample? What is the agreement, and does judge error differ by strategy?

Have you run the main comparison (or the 38-entry matched ablation) with a second, different model family as writer and/or as judge? If the ranking or the closeness of reading strategies changes, the main conclusion would change.
In the full-text-hiding experiment, what is the full-text coverage before the repair round, so that all three conditions are compared without repair?
How were the strategies developed? Which entries were inspected during prompt and pipeline design, and roughly how much iteration did each strategy receive?
What is the audit's false-flag rate on unaltered paragraphs, and how does it handle omission or misattribution errors?

For paragraph text beyond the reference facts (drafts make ~24 statements per paper vs. ~12 reference facts), can you estimate what fraction is correct and relevant, e.g. via the audit plus a human sample, so that coverage is not the only quality signal?

Is there a regime (larger reference lists, longer inputs, weaker model) where you expect or observed extract-then-write or agentic reading to outperform direct reading? The 30-75-reference tier is mentioned as exploratory; what does it show?
Given that curator text cannot be redistributed, how will other researchers reproduce the reference fact lists and scores exactly?
Limitations: The paper's limitations section is thorough and honest; the most consequential items (single model family, no human validation, narrow indirect reference, open-access-only text, no development split) should be weighed more heavily in the framing of the conclusions, particularly the claim that reading strategies are close.
The access result should be framed explicitly as partly a consequence of how the reference is constructed (curator text written from full text and supplements).
Results do not cover inputs larger than one prompt or weaker models, where strategy choice is most likely to matter.
